lessons.title: What a DBMS Does
lessons.concept: A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that stores, organizes, retrieves, and manages data while enforcing rules for consistency, security, and concurrent access. Compared to ad-hoc file storage, a DBMS provides structured schemas, query languages, transactions, and controlled multi-user access.
lessons.formula: Core responsibilities: data definition (schema), data manipulation (queries/updates), integrity constraints, concurrency control, recovery/backup, and access control.
lessons.worked_example: In a college system, student records, enrollments, and grades can be stored in tables with constraints (e.g., unique student_id, valid course references). A DBMS lets multiple staff query/update safely while preserving relationships and recovering from failures.
mistakes: Thinking a DBMS is only 'where data is stored' and ignoring integrity, concurrency, and recovery roles.
Confusing a database (the data) with a DBMS (the software managing it).
Assuming file systems provide the same transactional guarantees as a DBMS by default.

lessons.title: Keys and Relationships
lessons.concept: Keys identify rows and connect tables. A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table and should not be NULL. A candidate key is any column/set that could uniquely identify rows; one is chosen as primary. A foreign key in one table references a primary/candidate key in another table to enforce referential integrity.
lessons.formula: Primary key: unique + not null (per row identity). Foreign key: values must match referenced key values or be NULL if allowed by design.
lessons.worked_example: students(student_id PK, name), courses(course_id PK, title), enrollments(student_id FK, course_id FK, semester). enrollments.student_id must exist in students.student_id, preventing orphan enrollment records.
mistakes: Using non-unique or frequently changing attributes as primary keys without care.
Assuming foreign keys are optional for correctness (they are critical for referential integrity).
Confusing primary key (identity) with unique descriptive attributes that may change.

lessons.title: Normalization (Practical Basics)
lessons.concept: Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. In practice: 1NF requires atomic values (no repeating groups in a single column). 2NF removes partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF removes non-key attributes depending on other non-key attributes. The goal is consistency and maintainability, balanced with query performance needs.
lessons.formula: 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency (for composite keys). 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency among non-key attributes.
lessons.worked_example: If an orders table stores customer_name and customer_address repeated for every order, updating an address requires many rows. Better: customers(customer_id, name, address) and orders(order_id, customer_id, ...), linked by customer_id.
mistakes: Thinking normalization means 'split every table as much as possible' without considering use case.
Ignoring anomalies: update anomaly, insertion anomaly, deletion anomaly.
Confusing normalization levels or assuming 3NF eliminates all design trade-offs.

lessons.title: Transactions and ACID
lessons.concept: A transaction is a logical unit of work that must be treated as a whole (all-or-nothing in effect). ACID properties describe reliable transaction behavior: Atomicity (all or none), Consistency (moves database from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't improperly interfere), Durability (committed changes survive failures).
lessons.formula: Transaction control (common SQL): BEGIN/START TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT; or ROLLBACK; ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
lessons.worked_example: Transferring money: debit account A and credit account B. Both steps must succeed or both must be rolled back; otherwise money is lost/created. Atomicity ensures this all-or-nothing behavior.
mistakes: Assuming each SQL statement is automatically part of a larger multi-step transaction without explicit control (behavior depends on autocommit/settings).
Confusing consistency (rules/invariants preserved) with isolation (concurrency visibility).
Believing durability means 'never any failure' rather than 'committed data persists after commit despite crashes'.

practice.question: Which key uniquely identifies each row in a table and should not be NULL?
practice.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table and enforces entity integrity by not allowing NULL values (in standard relational design). A foreign key references a key in another table.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped.

practice.question: What is the main purpose of a foreign key?
practice.explanation: A foreign key creates a link between tables by referencing a primary/candidate key in another table, helping ensure that relationships remain valid (e.g., you cannot reference a non-existent parent record).
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped.

practice.question: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction is treated as all-or-nothing?
practice.explanation: Atomicity means either all operations in a transaction are applied, or none are. If any part fails, the transaction is rolled back to preserve a consistent state.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped.

practice.question: A table stores multiple phone numbers in a single column as '111,222,333'. This violates which normal form most directly?
practice.explanation: First Normal Form (1NF) requires atomic (indivisible) attribute values and no repeating groups in a single field. Storing multiple values in one column violates atomicity; a better design is a separate related table/rows for phone numbers.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped.

practice.question: Which statement best distinguishes a database from a DBMS?

options.A: Database is software; DBMS is the stored data
options.B: Database is the collection of data; DBMS is the software that manages it
options.C: Both terms mean exactly the same thing
options.D: DBMS is only a backup file format

practice.explanation: A database refers to the organized collection of data. A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software system used to create, access, manage, and secure that data.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped.

practice.question: Which of the following best describes a candidate key?

options.B: A minimal set of attributes that can uniquely identify a tuple
options.C: A key used only for sorting
options.D: A foreign key in another table

practice.explanation: A candidate key uniquely identifies rows and is minimal (no proper subset is unique). One candidate key is chosen as the primary key.

practice.question: Which anomaly occurs when deleting a row causes unintended loss of other important data due to poor design?
practice.explanation: A deletion anomaly happens when removing one fact (e.g. last student in a course) also removes unrelated facts stored only in that row. Proper normalization separates entities to avoid this.

questions.question: In a bank transfer transaction, money is debited from account A but not credited to account B due to a failure. Which property requires the system to undo the debit?
questions.explanation: Atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing execution of a transaction. If any step fails, completed steps in that transaction must be rolled back so partial effects do not persist.

questions.question: If every employee belongs to one department and department details are repeated in every employee row, updating a department's location may require many row updates. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: An update anomaly occurs when the same fact is stored redundantly in multiple places, so a change must be applied in many rows and inconsistency can occur if any are missed. Normalization (separating department data) reduces this risk.

questions.question: Which of the following can be a valid reason to choose a surrogate primary key (e.g., auto-increment id)?

options.B: It can provide a stable, simple unique identifier when natural attributes may change
options.C: It removes the need for foreign keys

questions.explanation: Surrogate keys are often used when natural keys are composite, long, or subject to change. They do not eliminate the need for foreign keys or guarantee normalization; they primarily provide a stable identifier.

questions.question: After a successful COMMIT, a power failure occurs. Which ACID property guarantees the committed changes are not lost?
questions.explanation: Durability ensures that once a transaction is committed, its effects persist in non-volatile storage and survive subsequent system failures.

questions.question: A relationship where one department has many employees is best represented by:

options.A: Storing all employee names in one department column
options.B: Putting a department_id foreign key in the employees table
options.C: Duplicating the departments table for each employee
options.D: Removing primary keys from both tables

questions.explanation: In a one-to-many relationship, the 'many' side (employees) typically stores a foreign key referencing the primary key of the 'one' side (departments). This preserves normalization and referential integrity.

questions.question: Which normal form removes transitive dependency of non-key attributes on the primary key (assuming 2NF)?
questions.explanation: Third Normal Form (3NF) requires that non-key attributes depend only on the key, not on other non-key attributes (no transitive dependency), given 1NF and 2NF are satisfied.

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures concurrent transactions do not lead to inconsistent intermediate visibility as per isolation level guarantees?
questions.explanation: Isolation controls how/when changes made by one transaction become visible to others, preventing unwanted interference; actual behavior depends on the isolation level.

questions.question: A table with a composite primary key (order_id, product_id) has a non-key attribute product_name depending only on product_id. This indicates violation related to:
questions.explanation: In 2NF, non-key attributes must depend on the whole composite key, not part of it. product_name depending only on product_id is a partial dependency, suggesting decomposition (e.g. a products table).
